opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a GPU only does useful work when it isn't waiting. In large training runs, every step depends on collective communication across thousands of accelerators, so the slowest link sets the pace for everyone. If one path is congested, or a link flaps, or a switch has a problem, you can end up with a whole cluster's worth of very expensive, very power-hungry silicon sitting idle while it waits on a handful of packets.

Traditional reliable transports tend to pin a flow to a single path through the network. That's simple, but it means you're vulnerable to hash collisions, where several big flows land on the same link while others sit underused, and to any single failure along that path. Multipath Reliable Connection spreads a connection's traffic across many paths simultaneously and handles reliability and ordering in a way that tolerates packets arriving via different routes. So you get much better use of the bandwidth you've already built, and you're far less sensitive to any one hot spot or broken component.

From a per-watt perspective, that matters in a few ways. First, the network itself is a significant chunk of capital and power, and if you can drive it closer to its real capacity, you get more communication per joule spent on optics and switches. Second, and more importantly, you shrink the tail latency of collectives, which directly reduces GPU idle time. The GPUs are drawing substantial power whether they're computing or stalled, so cutting stall time is basically free efficiency. Third, resilience: when a link goes bad, being able to route around it gracefully instead of slowing down or crashing a job means you lose less work to restarts and checkpoint recovery, which is pure wasted energy.

So the headline isn't that the network gets faster in some benchmark sense. It's that the whole system spends a larger fraction of its time, and its power budget, actually training the model. At the scale we're operating, even a few percent improvement in effective utilization translates into a lot of compute you didn't have to build or power.

r001.rationale: The response says MRC spreads traffic across many paths, but does not say this enables networks with fewer switch layers.

r002.rationale: The response links better network utilization and reduced GPU idle time to efficiency, but does not explain that reducing power spent on switching increases useful GPU work per watt.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that a GPU cluster's power budget is mostly fixed once you've built it. The GPUs draw their power whether they're doing useful math or sitting idle waiting on the network. So the question of work per watt is really a question of how much of the time the accelerators are actually busy. And at the scale we're training now, the network is one of the biggest reasons they aren't.

Traditional transports like plain RDMA over Converged Ethernet put a single flow on a single path. If that path gets congested, or a link flaps, or a switch has a bad day, that one flow stalls. And because training is a synchronous, collective operation, one stalled flow means thousands of GPUs sit at a barrier burning power and producing nothing. That's the worst possible outcome from an efficiency standpoint.

Multipath Reliable Connection changes that picture in a few ways. First, by spraying packets across many paths simultaneously, you get much better load balancing across the fabric. You're not relying on hashing to spread flows evenly, which never really works for the large, elephant-style flows you see in all-reduce or all-to-all. So you can run the links closer to their actual capacity instead of leaving headroom to absorb hash collisions. That's fewer switches and fewer optics doing the same job, which is real watts saved on the network side.

Second, the reliability piece means a failed or degraded path doesn't become a job-level event. The transport reroutes around it, retransmits what it needs to, and the application keeps going. Every time you avoid a checkpoint restore or a stalled iteration, that's minutes of a multi-megawatt cluster not being wasted.

Third, and this is the subtler one, MRC lets you handle out-of-order delivery in hardware rather than in software. Once you accept that packets are going to arrive out of order because they took different paths, you can design the NIC to reassemble efficiently without the host CPU or the GPU getting involved. That keeps the compute focused on compute.

So if I had to summarize it: MRC doesn't make the GPUs faster. It makes them wait less. And at the power levels we're talking about, waiting less is the single biggest lever on useful work per watt that we have.

r001.rationale: The response says better load balancing can mean fewer switches, but does not state that this enables networks with fewer switch layers.

r002.rationale: It says fewer switches save network power and separately says reduced GPU waiting improves work per watt, but does not connect lower switching power to increased useful GPU work per watt.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it in terms of how much of the time the GPUs are doing useful computation versus waiting for data. If you have a large distributed job, a delay in one part of the network can leave a lot of GPUs waiting, and those GPUs are still consuming power.

The opportunity with Multipath Reliable Connection is to use multiple network paths so that congestion or a problem on one path doesn’t become a bottleneck for the whole job. If that reduces communication stalls, you can get more useful computation out of the same GPUs over the same period of time.

That doesn’t automatically mean better performance per watt—you have to account for the power used by the network, too. The measure I’d care about is how much energy it takes to finish the workload. If MRC helps the cluster finish sooner without a comparable increase in power, that’s a real efficiency gain.

r001.rationale: It says MRC uses multiple network paths to reduce bottlenecks, but does not state that this enables networks with fewer switch layers.

r002.rationale: It discusses reduced communication stalls and energy to finish a workload, but does not explain that less power spent on switching increases useful GPU work per watt.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a GPU consumes power even when it’s waiting for data. So the question is: how much of the energy going into the cluster actually turns into useful computation?

Multipath Reliable Connection can help by letting communication use multiple paths through the network. If one path is congested or has a failure, you have other ways to deliver that data reliably. That can reduce the time GPUs spend waiting on communication, particularly in a synchronized workload where one slow transfer can hold up a whole group of GPUs.

So the benefit isn’t necessarily that any individual GPU draws fewer watts. It’s that, for the power you’re already spending on the cluster, you can get more useful work done. How much more depends on whether communication is actually the bottleneck and how well the transport uses those available paths.

r001.rationale: The response says MRC can use multiple network paths, but does not connect that capability to networks needing fewer switch layers.

r002.rationale: It says MRC may reduce GPU waiting and yield more useful work for the cluster’s power, but does not attribute this to reduced power spent on switching.
